clinician.trajectory_summary: A 53-year-old incarcerated Hispanic male with a 2-month history of vague abdominal pain, fatigue, easy bruising, and spontaneous epistaxis presented to the hospital from jail with acute worsening abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, and focal peritonitis 4 days after sustaining blunt abdominal trauma (multiple strikes to the abdomen). Initial laboratory evaluation revealed marked leukocytosis (WBC 38.4 × 10^9/L) and marked thrombocytosis (platelets 691 × 10^9/L), which were atypical for simple post-traumatic complications. CT imaging of the abdomen demonstrated a pancreatic hematoma with hemoperitoneum. The patient underwent emergent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a nearly severed distal pancreas and devascularized colon, necessitating distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and colonic resection with primary anastomosis. Subsequent bone marrow biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of CML, chronic phase, demonstrating slightly hypercellular marrow (70%) with trilineage hematopoiesis, mild myeloid hyperplasia, mild megakaryocytic hyperplasia, and molecular evidence of BCR/ABL+ fusion. Peripheral blood smear confirmed severe leukocytosis and thrombocytosis without circulating blasts. The patient was initiated on hydroxyurea with transition to imatinib (400 mg daily) for CML-directed therapy. The acute abdominal catastrophe was precipitated by blunt trauma in the setting of underlying, previously undiagnosed CML.
